newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity prices end slightly higher.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity prices end slightly higher.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures prices ended slightly higher Monday with some support from hot weather forecasts and increasing physical power prices, industry sources said.

September Palo Verde (PV) closed four cents higher at $31.81 per megawatt hour (MWh) following exchanges at $31.75-32.95, while October closed up 20 cents at $24.30 per MWh after hitting a new contract high of $25.10 and trading as low as $24.25 per MWh.
Remaining PV deferreds ended steady to 80 cents higher.

September California Oregon Border (COB) settled up 20 cents at the day's low of $23.60 following exchanges as high as $24.25, while October ended up six cents at $23.01 after exchanges at $23.00-23.40 per MWh.
NYMEX said an estimated total of 388 COB and 629 PV contracts traded.

Daily prices were said to be firmer, with peak firm COB electricity for Tuesday quoted at $20.50-23.00 per MWh, compared with $19.00-20.00 for Saturday/Monday combination sales. Firm, peak PV electricity for Tuesday was quoted at $40.00-44.00, compared with $32.00-45.00 for Saturday/Monday.

Forecasters called for the Northwest to be five to 10 degrees Fahrenheit above normal through Thursday in the western areas, with eastern areas like Wyoming and eastern Montana averaging five to 10 degrees below normal, Weather Services Corp said.

In the Southwest, temperatures were forecast to average two to five degrees above normal in the south, four to eight degrees below normal in the east including central Colorado, and near normal along the West Coast for the same period.

The 750 megawatt (MW) unit 5 at the Four Corners coal-fired power plant in New Mexico, shut late Thursday for repairs, was back to full power by late Saturday, a spokeswoman for the plant said Monday.
The plant's other 750 MW unit, as well as its 220 MW and two 185 MW units, were said to be operating normally.

Also, the 750 MW unit 3 at the Navajo coal-fired power plant near Page, Ariz., was scheduled to restart Monday afternoon after being shut over the weekend for repairs. Navajo's other two 750 MW units were said to be operating normally.

Separately, southbound transmission capacity on the Pacific Intertie will be cut by 350 MW to 850 MW during certain hours on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday of this week, according to the Bonneville Power Administration (BPA).
